sources.cite: IETF RFC 9989, Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC), May 2026 (obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091)
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-16 (the first half of the page). Relevant text: p=none, 'The Domain Owner offers no expression of preference'; p=quarantine, 'The Domain Owner considers such mail to be suspicious'; p=reject, failures are 'a clear indication that the use of the domain name is not valid'. A message passes DMARC when SPF or DKIM gives an aligned pass: 'Only an SPF-Authenticated Identifier that has Identifier Alignment with the Author Domain is enough'; a message 'is considered to produce a DMARC "pass" result if any DKIM-Authenticated Identifier aligns with the Author Domain.' There is 'currently no generally accepted mechanism' to list authorized third-party signing domains, so third parties must send aligned. Domain owners usually start at p=none and use aggregate reports to find every sending source, fixing legitimate streams before enforcement. The pct tag of RFC 7489 is gone (replaced by the t test flag), so the scenario does not use it.

Fictional company and people. Domains use the reserved .example top-level domain (IETF RFC 2606) and addresses the documentation range 198.51.100.0/24 (IETF RFC 5737). The payment amount, cutoff and payslip run are the author's.

brief.situation: You are the security analyst at Halden Supply, a fictional wholesaler. At 09:00 a finance clerk forwards an email from the CEO's address asking her to wire $48,000 to a new supplier account before the bank's 10:30 cutoff. The mail gateway shows 37 such messages to finance staff. Payslips for 412 staff go out by email at 11:00 through PayrollCo, an outside service.
handover: haldensupply.example publishes a DMARC record with p=none and sends aggregate reports to the security team.
The CEO is travelling but answers his known mobile number.
howItWorks: The console shows alerts, mail and DNS events as they arrive, and what is at stake.
Each task takes your time: start it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The attacker and the bank keep working on the same clock.
When you close the incident, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The bank's wire cutoff is 10:30, 90 minutes after the 09:00 start.

How many minutes each command or task takes, and when the fictional problem spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. A second wave to accounts payable arrives 20 minutes in.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Uses the headers (SPF fail, no DKIM, DMARC fail at p=none, look-alike Reply-To) to show exact-domain spoofing from outside, not a compromised mailbox.
parts.modelAnswer: Authentication-Results showed SPF failing for 198.51.100.40, no DKIM and a DMARC fail that p=none let through; replies went to a look-alike domain. The CEO's account was not involved.

parts.label: First moves
parts.criteria: Stops the money first by an out-of-band check before the cutoff, then quarantines spoofs at the gateway and purges the mailboxes.
parts.modelAnswer: I had finance hold the wire and confirmed with the CEO on his known number, added a gateway rule for mail claiming our domain that fails DMARC, and purged the delivered messages.

parts.label: Enforcement
parts.criteria: Reads the aggregate reports before enforcing, aligns the legitimate third-party sender, then moves to quarantine or reject.
parts.modelAnswer: The reports showed PayrollCo sending unaligned payslips. PayrollCo now signs with DKIM as our domain, and only then did I publish p=quarantine, so forgeries are junked by receivers while payslips pass.

scoring.modelReasoning: The headers show exact-domain spoofing from 198.51.100.40: SPF fails, there is no DKIM, DMARC fails, and p=none tells receivers nothing, so they deliver it; replies go to a look-alike domain. First hold the wire with an out-of-band call before the 10:30 cutoff, then quarantine inbound mail that claims the domain and fails DMARC at the gateway and purge what was delivered. The gateway protects only your own staff; to stop forgeries reaching suppliers the domain must enforce. The aggregate reports show PayrollCo sending payslips as the domain without alignment, so have it sign with DKIM as d=haldensupply.example first, then publish p=quarantine (moving to reject after more report review). Warn finance and suppliers, and record that legitimate senders are aligned before enforcement.
